title: Pavan guru under an orange sky
hookLine: clean air as a gift and a duty
carry: air is the guru: every life begins with breath
tomorrow: Bebe and Mrs. Haddad meet over a garden hose. who wins?

cards: Wildfire smoke rolled in overnight. The sky is a flat orange, the sun a pink coin, and the air quality app on everyone's phone has turned purple. School cancels outdoor practice.
Across the hall, Arjan's little sister Jasleen has been coughing since breakfast.
Simran is helping hand out masks when she remembers what her dad's trucks do every morning at the yard: idle, for an hour, engines running so the cabs stay warm. Nobody ever thought about it.
Today everyone is thinking about breathing.

teach.h: PAVAN GURU: AIR IS THE GURU.
teach.b: The Japji's last lines, on Ang 8, call the air a Guru: pavan guru. That's more than a nice image, because of what a Guru is. A Guru is someone you receive from, depend on, and would never insult.
Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.
In Siddh Gosht, a long conversation with wandering yogis, they ask Guru Nanak where it all begins. His answer starts with breath.

In paraphrase: from the air, the breath, is the beginning; the Shabad is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. So the first thing every life receives is air, before milk, before a name.
And it's shared without a ticket. Jasleen breathes the same air as the people across the hall, the drivers at the yard, the firefighters up on the ridge.

teach.h: ONE SKY FOR THE WHOLE FAMILY.
teach.b: One sky, one breath, for the whole human family.

teach.h: A GIFT, AND SO A DUTY.
teach.b: That's why the gift comes with a duty.
If air is the Guru, then fouling it is like talking over your teacher, and keeping it clean is a kind of respect. Not one big gesture; small, ordinary choices.
Simran texts her dad, Harjit: could the drivers shut the engines off at the yard? Three dots. Then: I'll talk to them this week.
It's not a yes. It's a start.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji, which closes by calling the air a Guru, in their morning prayers, and some treat caring for the air and the earth as seva.

games.q: what does “air is the guru” mean?
o: the breath every life begins with: a gift, and a duty
the idea that only outdoor prayers really count
a Guru who taught by blowing a conch at dawn

games.q: the breath and the Guru — tap the pairs.
p: the Guru; attention is the disciple

s: calling air a Guru is only poetry, with no duty in it
a Guru is someone you receive from and would never insult; that makes clean air a kind of respect.
in Siddh Gosht, Guru Nanak's answer about the beginning starts with breath
in paraphrase: from the air, the breath, is the beginning; the Shabad is the Guru.
the air is the Guru only for people who pray
it's shared without a ticket: one sky, one breath, for everyone.

games.q: every school pickup, a friend's mom idles her car for twenty minutes to keep it cool. you're getting a ride. going by today, what fits best?
o: kindly ask if she'd mind switching off while you wait.
say nothing; one car can't make any real difference.
post about idling online without naming anyone.
games.why: air is the Guru, shared by everyone: the duty shows up in small, ordinary choices, asked kindly, like Simran's text to her dad.

practice: If the air where you are is clean enough, walk slowly for a minute, across a room, down a hall, or outside, and feel each breath arrive and leave. Notice it's the same air your neighbors are breathing.
Then stand still and let a few breaths be a quiet thank-you to the Guru you can't see.

wordCard.voice: Air is the Guru. Pavan guru, from the Japji's last lines: the breath every life begins with, a gift shared by all, and a duty to keep clean.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pavan, air or breath. Pavan guru: the Japji's last lines (Ang 8).

carryVoice: Something to keep: air is the guru, and every life begins with breath. Orange sky, three dots, day 1734.
